summary.oneLiner: A South India-based manufacturer of printing & writing paper (with wet lap pulp) operating two mills at Erode and Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu, selling into domestic and export (notably US) markets.
summary.business: Seshasayee Paper and Boards manufactures paper — chiefly printing & writing / copier grades — and wet lap pulp at two units in Tamil Nadu, Erode and Tirunelveli, selling to domestic and export markets (with the US a key export destination). The company also undertakes limited trading activity in petroleum products and note books alongside its core paper business.

currentContext.strengths: Product diversification / depth across paper grades lets the company retune product-mix to counter cheaper imports and shifting demand, credited for a resilient domestic sales performance despite intense import competition|Flexibility and agility in adapting product mix to dynamic market conditions, evidenced by highest-ever annual domestic sales (2,28,955 tonnes) in FY26 despite challenging conditions|Conversion-capacity upgrade (new sheeter at Erode) enabling supply of high-realisation copier products to the US market, supporting a rebound in exports in Q4FY26|Stable industrial relations — the 10th five-year wage settlement for the Erode unit was concluded during FY26, valid through 31.03.2029, giving multi-year labour-cost certainty
currentContext.strategies: Product diversification strategy: retune product-mix flexibly and with agility to counter cheaper imports and dynamic market conditions, credited for the company's resilient domestic sales performance|Upgrade conversion capacity toward high-realisation grades — commissioning of an additional sheeter at Erode to supply high-realisation copier products to the US market|Continued cost reduction / optimisation efforts to defend operating margins against realisation pressure|Continue tree farming activity to support quality wood/fibre supply (raw-material security), per Board's Report reference to ongoing tree farming programme|The Board follows a Dividend Distribution Policy adopted under SEBI (LODR) Regulation 43A, published on the company's website, under which a per-share dividend is recommended annually to shareholders.
currentContext.expansion: The company completed Mill Development Plan-III (MDP-III) at Unit: Erode in phases during FY2020-21 and FY2021-22, which augmented Erode's annual installed paper capacity to 1,65,000 tonnes; Unit: Tirunelveli's installed capacity remains unchanged at 90,000 tonnes, taking total installed capacity to 2,55,000 tonnes per annum. During FY26 the company successfully commissioned an additional sheeter at Unit: Erode, augmenting conversion capacity to supply high-realisation copier products to the US market. No new capacity-expansion project (beyond the completed MDP-III and the FY26 sheeter) is described in this bundle.
currentContext.mdna: Domestic packaging boards (corrugated, carton board, duplex) growing 8-9% p.a., driven by e-commerce, food delivery and organised retail|Printing & Writing segment stabilising after years of digitisation pressure, with NEP 2020-driven school enrollment providing a partial offset|Tissue and hygiene paper growing 7-8% as middle-class penetration deepens|Newsprint in secular decline at (-)4-5% p.a.|Cheaper duty-free imports from China and Indonesia remain the industry's biggest pain point; GST 2.0 reforms (Sep'25) with NIL GST on notebook paper temporarily gave imported paper a 12-15% cost advantage over domestic production, before market prices settled in Q4 at levels below pre-reform prices|US tariff-related disruption suspended exports to the US from May'25-Sep'25, forcing extra volumes into an already import-pressured domestic market and steepening the realisation decline; post the US Supreme Court's tariff decision, stability has been restored to export volumes and the outlook for this segment is favourable|Global supply-chain volatility — escalation of the US-Iran conflict and Strait of Hormuz disruption in early 2026 — has raised the cost of imported pulp, waste paper, chemicals and coal, expected to significantly affect margins in H1FY27|International paper prices from Indonesia and China remain weak with no signs of recovery|FY27 industry consensus is for a 6-7% CAGR in paper consumption, led by packaging/paperboard (e-commerce, FMCG, quick-commerce) and with printing & writing paper gaining traction from NEP 2020 implementation and rising textbook/competitive-exam volumes; tissue & hygiene paper expected to grow at double-digit rates|FY27 expected to be a watershed year for sustainable packaging adoption — phased EPR norm rollout, brand plastic-substitution mandates and demand for FSC-certified/food-grade/recyclable paperboard reshaping product mix, with specialty papers (release liners, thermal, decor, filter, food-service grades) seeing double-digit growth and higher realisations for mills with R&D, certifications and downstream relationships

risks.note: Surging cheap paper imports from ASEAN and China (ASEAN imports up ~250% and Chinese imports up ~181% over two years) enter largely duty-free under AIFTA, at an estimated USD 40-50/tonne versus India's ~USD 110/tonne cost of production — a gap domestic producers cannot bridge without trade protection; only a temporary MIP on VPB has been imposed so far and broader safeguard duties are still being sought by the industry.

risks.risk: Wood fibre scarcity and cost escalation
risks.note: Wood availability in Tamil Nadu/South India is acutely tight, with Casuarina and Eucalyptus prices escalating due to competition from plywood, MDF and particle-board industries and new pulp mill capacities; the company's own SWOT also flags a large government-owned competitor in the same state competing aggressively for wood sourcing.

risks.risk: Currency risk raising imported input costs
risks.note: Steep INR depreciation over the last five years benefits exports but raises the cost of imported coal, chemicals and market pulp, an integrated-mill input-cost exposure.
Erratic monsoons and reduced water flows in the River Cauvery are flagged as a structural concern for the company's Tamil Nadu-based mills.

risks.risk: Structural digitisation pressure on Printing & Writing paper
risks.note: Newsprint and the P&W segment face secular decline from digital media, e-invoicing and digital documentation, only partly offset by education-sector demand; the pace is slower in India than mature markets but the headwind is structural.

risks.risk: Import dependency for key inputs at Unit II/III
risks.note: Company's own SWOT flags dependency on imported pulp / waste-paper for Unit-II/III and on imported coal, plus non-availability of indigenous coal — exposing operating costs to global commodity and freight cycles.

The US is the company's major export market; US tariff-related disruptions suspended exports there from May'25-Sep'25 in FY26, forcing volumes into an already import-pressured domestic market — illustrating the concentration risk even though stability has since been restored.

risks.risk: Scale and vintage disadvantage versus larger/global players
risks.note: Company's own SWOT cites lack of size and multiple machines as a high-cost disadvantage, and older machines/buildings, versus the scale and cost advantages the industry associates with larger integrated producers.

one-line thesis: Despite severe market headwinds from duty-free paper imports and elevated wood costs, Seshasayee delivered resilient FY24 performance with record production and nil net debt, positioning itself for growth via strategic asset acquisition and 20% capacity expansion in Erode, though near-term margins remain pressured until FY25 recovery.
financial scorecard: rev: +1.5% YoY; EBITDA: -28% YoY; PAT: -33% YoY; orderbook: N/A; netdebt: ₹0
guidance: Expecting challenging market conditions for W&P grades until Q2FY25, with recovery anticipated in H2FY25; full-year FY25 PAT guidance not provided, but management expects improved performance post-capacity augmentation and import duty intervention.
segment / subsidiary detail: Erode unit produced 1.65 lakh tonnes (highest ever), contributing ~69% of total production; Fine Paper segment to be expanded via Servalakshmi acquisition (75,000 tonnes pa); Writing & Printing grades dominate revenue but face pricing pressure; pulp self-sufficiency remains core strategic focus.
growth verticals / optionality: 20% capacity augmentation at Erode unit (pending environment clearance); integration of Servalakshmi unit (75ktpa fine paper) by FY26; potential for export market penetration if import duties are imposed; agro-forestry expansion to secure 100% wood supply.
margins & cost dynamics: EBITDA margin compressed due to 40-50% wood cost inflation (Tamil Nadu-specific); realisation down 15-20% YoY on W&P grades due to Chinese/ASEAN imports; cost recovery expected only if import duties are imposed or wood supply stabilizes.
capex / expansion: ₹350-400 crore planned over 2 years: ₹200-250 crore for Erode unit expansion (20%); ₹150 crore for Servalakshmi unit refurbishment; funded entirely by internal accruals (nil net debt policy maintained).
capital allocation: 100% internal funding; no debt raised; dividend payout of ₹5/share (250% of face value) maintained despite capex; no buyback announced; retained earnings fully deployed into capex and tree farming initiatives.
risks & watch-items: Duty-free paper imports (up 68% YoY, China +181%, ASEAN +247%); wood scarcity and price volatility; delayed NCLAT clearance for Servalakshmi acquisition; prolonged margin pressure until H2FY25; lack of BIS/QCO enforcement on imported paper.
management quality / tone: Cautiously optimistic; acknowledges severe headwinds but emphasizes operational resilience, strategic capex, and ESG leadership; strong emphasis on lobbying for import duties and land access for plantations; confident in long-term growth despite short-term pain.
non-obvious takeaways: Company plants 115 crore seedlings over 7 years — equivalent to 1.3 lakh acres — creating a de facto raw material monopoly via contract farming; this vertical integration is more strategic than any capacity expansion; also, 90% of wood is sourced from 5 lakh farmers — making SPB a rural employment engine, not just a paper maker.
